analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in number 35 original, the United States against Maine and others. Mr. Claiborne, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, it may please the court. This case and the next are original cases in the technical sense, that is to say, they begin and end in this court on the court's original docket. But they're original cases in a more colloquial sense as well. The main ground of decision in each of the cases is, in our view, novel, indeed dangerously so. In both cases, the principal question is whether what nature made an island is, in the eye of the law, somewhat perversely, a peninsula. In the first of these cases, that question arises in respect of Long Island, which one might think everyone other than lawyers and judges would know is indeed the island that it's called. An island in law as well as in fact. Why we must debate this seemingly silly question is that the result affects the extent of the submerged lands belonging to Rhode Island and New York as distinguished from the submerged lands of the United States. That arises because under a venerable doctrine, the states, each of them on the coast, own the beds and banks of all inland navigable waters within their boundaries. And by virtue of the Sumerical Lands Act of 1953, they likewise own an additional three-mile belt measured from the outer limit of those inland waters. Mr. Claiborne, does the case also relate to who has jurisdiction over the water or may regulate traffic on the water or fishing? It does not, Justice White. This case is entirely under the Submerged Lands Act, and that act simply governs the seabed and the resources thereof, the right to extract minerals and the right to take resources but not fishing within that zone. But they're not, but if Long Island Sound is inland waters, it's not international waters then either. It would, I must say that most of Long Island Sound is at all events by common ground inland water. That is so in the view of the United States because it's historic inland water. That is so in the view of the two states opposite because it's a juridical battle. To the extent it isn't though, does it affect who has jurisdiction over the navigable waters? Whether it's inland or whether it's territorial sea of the state, it would seem to me has little effect on its jurisdictional powers in that area. But it's open sea though. If it's open sea, then the state would have no claim to govern other than its own citizens within that zone. Well, there's some of that involved here, I take it. And there is in Block Island Sound some of that involved. And indeed, this dispute originally arose because of Rhode Island's claim to control pilots bringing both domestic and domestic. So that is involved to that extent. It is involved to that extent, though it isn't, strictly speaking, the bone of contention here. Mr. Clavin, along that line of questioning, your brief states that there are international implications, but I don't think they were identified in the brief. What are they, really? Justice Powell, to the extent that there are, that this court should declare that, for instance, that all of Block Island Sound is territorial water and not high seas, the sea lanes between Block Island and the Rhode Island mainland on the east and between Block Island and Long Island on the west would be open to, would not be open sea and would not be freely navigated by the world community, but only subject to a right of innocent passage and otherwise by permission of the coastal states. And to that extent, to the extent that this court's decision is viewed because it's an interpretation of international law, international convention, it would have international radiations. Would the position of the United States bring international waters closer to the mainland than the United States? It would, to some extent, in due to your position with respect to Block Island Sound, wouldn't it? That is so, and that is generally so. It is generally the position of the United States to favor the freedom of the high seas. May I just follow up? What effect would it have on fishing rights, on electronic surveillance by other countries, and on mineral rights internationally? With respect to the latter two, Justice Powell, I think I'm correct in saying that it would have no effect on fishing rights or on the right to exploit the subsoil of the sea, because in both those respects, the United States has declared for itself ownership of a zone which goes either 200 miles out or to the edge of the continental shelf. And therefore, these areas, now in dispute, would in no event be open to international exploitation or to international fishery, except by permission or by treaty. With respect to surveillance, I suppose that that would be affected in that so long as these are high seas, any vessel can come in those waters, provided it's not for fishing and provided it's not for the purpose of exploiting the seabed. To what extent does that work both ways? In other words, I suppose your concern, I mean, the government is concerned about a precedent that would involve similar situations in other parts of the world. Justice Stevens, you have hit upon the reason why it has traditionally been the policy of the United States, as a matter of international relations, to confine the high seas close to shore, relatively close to shore, because of the interest of the United States in avoiding or wanting to avoid setting a precedent which other nations can imitate and thereby close off the areas near their borders to international navigation and as well to our surveillance of their activities. It is, as Your Honor says, a two-way street. Well, the government surely isn't concerned about any navigation problems as between it and the states, is it? Because certainly the federal government can regulate to its heart's content in that area. I think that is so, Justice Rehnquist. As I've indicated in answer to a question from Justice White, that it is common ground in this case that if Long Island is not an extension of the mainland, then the inland waters behind Long Island are restricted to what is known as Long Island Sound proper. If I can refer the court to our exceptions, at the back there are three charts. The first one would indicate sufficiently what I mean by Long Island Sound proper. On chart one, the court will notice that Long Island Sound, the eastern portion of it, is indicated, and that it's closed off by a line from Orient Point on the north of the east end of Long Island to Fishers Island to Napatry Point. The area west of that is Long Island Sound proper, and it is common ground that that area is inland water, not because it satisfies the test as a juridical bay, but because it has and always has been historic inland waters of the United States, and that claim by the United States inures to the benefit of the neighboring states, for the most part, New York in this case. What is in dispute is the area indicated as Block Island Sound to the east. If Long Island is not an extension of the mainland, no part of Block Island Sound qualifies as part of a bay or as otherwise inland water. There's no claim in this case at this stage that those waters are historic inland waters. Mr. Claiborne, what is it about Block Island Sound that the United States says does not make it an historic bay, whereas Long Island Sound is, in your view? Justice O'Connor, it appears that at the time when the claim to Block Island Sound matured as a historic claim, the general rule, though it was not properly speaking a rule, but the tendency was to treat waters which were closable by a line something approaching 10 miles only would fit that description. And that line at the north between Orient Point and Fisher Island and Naphti Point is a total of less than 10 miles. While a line from Montauk Point to Watch Hill, much less a line which would include Block Island, would exceed 10 miles and indeed in one case come to 24 or nearby, 24 miles. Accordingly, those waters were not historically viewed as sufficiently enclosed to justify a claim of historic inland water. And as a matter of fact, the evidence, so it appears, does not justify such a claim for Block Island Sound. And the two states in whose interest it would have been to extend the historic claim that far, having not sought to do so, presumably for good reason. Now, just to identify the position of the parties further, as the court sees on this chart one, is the position of the United States. That is, Long Island not being an extension of the mainland, there is no juridical bay. There is only the historic inland waters of Long Island Sound. And some subsidiary bays, such as Gardiner's Bay, which qualify under the convention. And accordingly, the line which borders, which is the boundary of inland waters, includes no part of Block Island Sound. The only portion of Block Island Sound which would appertain to the two states are those portions which constitute the three-mile belt, which by virtue of the Sumerital Lands Act was granted to them in 1953. The special master in this case, having concluded to reach a middle solution, as is perhaps all too often the case, drew a line which first he concluded that Long Island was an extension of the mainland, and then he closed the bay formed by that island. This is illustrated in the third of our charts. He drew a line from Montauk Point, almost directly due north to Watch Hill Point, and thereby enclosed some portion of Block Island Sound. We agree with the master that if Long Island is an extension of the mainland, which we deny, that is the correct closing point. Finally, the position of the two states is illustrated in chart two. They would first maintain that Long Island is indeed an extension of the mainland, but they would then close the bay, which they say is formed thereby, by drawing a line not north but east to Block Island, and then a northerly line from Block Island to Point Judas. Mr. Claiborne, what is the standard of review that this court traditionally uses in reviewing the findings of fact of a special master? If your honor, please, the most recent statement by the court itself with respect to that matter arises in Colorado versus New Mexico, number 80 original, decided June 4th of this year. In that case, the court indicated that the master's findings deserve respect and tacit, I'm reading from page 6 of the slip opinion, and a tacit presumption of correctness, but the ultimate responsibility for deciding what are correct findings of fact remains with us. The court then cites one of its previous decisions in Mississippi versus Arkansas at 415 of the United States reports, and concludes, upon our independent review of the record, we find that Colorado has failed to meet its burden. I read those words of the court as indicating that this court has concluded that he ought not review a master's finding as though they were the findings of a district judge sitting as a district court, but except for matters of credibility, where his appraisal of the witnesses must obviously be given more weight than what can be determined on a cold record. This court has an obligation to review the evidence to the extent that it is challenged. Here, we say that the court need go no further than the master's report because we accept every finding in that report, and so far as I'm aware, there's no challenge to any finding of fact in that report by a counsel opposite. Accordingly, there's very little occasion in this particular case for the court to do more than look at the evidence as summarized by the master. Now, the question whether Long Island is an extension of the mainland, which is the dispositive question in this case, is one that has tended only recently to arise, and to arise all too often. It's a troubling development that every island somewhere near shore is now sort of attended it for being treated as not an island, but a peninsula. If that tendency were to continue unabated, the number of challenges and the original document of this court would be severely burdened. Our brief traces the history of this notion that an island can sometimes be viewed, not as an island jurisdictionally, but as an extension of the mainland mass. It was intended as a very narrow exception to the rule of geography. It was originally applied only in the Louisiana Delta, in the Mississippi Delta in Louisiana, where the land mass is so crisscrossed by canals, it looks like a jigsaw puzzle, somewhat separated, and the court concluded, almost unavoidably, that if one were to take each of those waterways and treat it as separating the mass into islands, Louisiana would wash into the sea. Accordingly, in that special circumstance, it was deemed appropriate, and this was in a case called Louisiana v. Mississippi in 1905, in which this court said, to be sure these are technical islands, speaking of the St. Bernard Peninsula, but we must view it as part of the land mass. The only other way in which the court has thought it proper to treat islands as part of the land, part of the land mass, is when a usually small mud lump, or rather a luvial formation, was appended to the mainland in the sense that it looked like it had dropped off, like a teardrop. There was a narrow channel separating it from the mainland. Mr. Claiborne, may I ask you this question? Does transatlantic shipping use Long Island sound? The indications in the record, Justice Powell, are that little transatlantic shipping, mostly coastal shipping, but a very heavy volume of coastal shipping, and a very much navigated, the total volume I've forgotten, but the volume is quite substantial, and the channel is some 35 feet deep. 35 feet. That could accommodate transatlantic shipping. It could indeed. Now, it so happens that the port of New York is mostly to the west rather than on the East River, and therefore the traffic doesn't go through the East River, and there is no substantial international port within Long Island Sound. Mr. Claiborne, may I ask in your discussion of the islands that you were involved in, what is the government's position with respect to Manhattan Island? Mr. Stephen, we don't have to resolve that question here, because as it happens, whichever way one treats Manhattan, the result is the same. The record in this case does indicate that the geographer of the State Department, when asked that question in deposition, he died before the trial, and therefore his deposition was introduced in evidence. His answer was that Manhattan, and indeed Staten Island as well, were treated by the committee, the baseline committee, which drew the coastline of the United States as water, as islands, and therefore as water, because under the rule of Article 7, an island wholly within an indentation is treated as water. But that is only true with respect to an island, not with respect to some portion of the landmass. It is obviously a closer question whether Staten Island and Manhattan Island are islands for all purposes. The case of Long Island is much clearer, because there the separation is some seven-tenths of a mile. We have a channel, which is a tidal channel, not a river, and we have a channel thirty-five foot deep, and we have it very actively navigated. When one compares it to an instance which the court rejected in the Louisiana context, the Ile d'Harnier and what was claimed to be Caillou Bay, there we had a channel that was only a third, not even a third of a mile wide, only some fourteen feet deep, and carrying a far lesser value of seagoing traffic. Mr. Klayman, what about coastal shipping coming from Boston to the port of New York? I suppose it would actually be a little bit shorter if it went through Long Island Sound. Does the record show anything about whether coastal shipping coming from east of Block Island goes through the Sound on its way to New York or whether it goes south of Long Island? I think, Justice Rehnquist, the record indicates that it does not go through the Sound, that most of that traffic goes round. Now, why that should be so, because I think you're almost correct that the distance is marginally shorter. Well, other than perhaps it was just thought not to be a very suitable place to navigate. Right, and there may be some sense of congestion even in the... The state of the East of Boston said it was heavily, that passageway, seven-tenths of a mile, was heavily navigated by what? By commercial vessels. From where? Not coastal vessels? They are coastal vessels, but I'm only suggesting that they may not be coming from Boston. They may be. bringing goods to and from ports within the Sound itself. Sure, and so it is heavily navigated by coastal vessels. It is heavily navigated by commercial coastal vessels, no question about that. Which have a destination at a port somewhere on the Sound. Yes, and the master's report is quite clear as to the exact volume of that traffic. But the sound is... The passageway is navigated by vessels going from New York Harbor up to destinations on the Sound or from Sound origins into New York. I think in both directions, yes. Let me say that the master seemed to have recognized that he was straining the normal rules in treating Long Island or would be in treating Long Island as an extension of the main... Mr. Clayton, how many harbors do you have on the Sound? Your Honor, I should know but don't. I take it there are Connecticut harbors there as well as some in Rhode Island and Long Island itself. There's a harbor in Long Island. I frankly don't know as I certainly should know what harbors there are there but the volume of traffic indicates that there must be some place to disembark the cargo and to bring it on board. Now, as I say, the master seemed to have recognized the difficulty especially in light of this court's actual rulings as opposed to its language in the Louisiana case in treating Long Island which very severely deflects the coast if it's treated as an extension of the mainland as an extension rather than an island. So, what he did was to say to himself but when I look at what Long Island does it's clear to me that what is behind Long Island looks like a bay and therefore since it seems to form a bay and the only way it can do so legally I will treat it as an extension of the mainland. Totally backward reasoning result-oriented reasoning He said this area of Long Island is used as a bay it looks like a bay therefore it must be a bay yet it cannot be a bay unless Long Island is an extension of the mainland therefore I will treat Long Island as an extension of the mainland even though it may not qualify otherwise. Now, that is our bone of contention with the master's report and if that sort of principle that sort of loose principle were to be encouraged we would have many more such cases there are many other states waiting in the wings to see whether this novel effort prevails. I say what time I have for a while. Mr. Pound-Fitz. Mr. Chief Justice may it please the court I will respond to the government's arguments with respect to whether or not there is a bay as found by the master and Mr. Doherty will address the proper closing lines for that bay. The master found a juridical bay as he inevitably had to do on the basis of the facts and the law. There were four basic reasons why he found a juridical bay. First of all the area is geographically a bay. Secondly it meets all the requirements of Article 7 of the Convention on the Territorial Sea and Contiguous Zone. Thirdly it satisfies the use and purpose concept in international law that concept which permits a bay to be closed. And fourthly Long Island meets the requirements as set forth by this court in the Louisiana boundary case of being realistically considered as part of the mainland. Of course if you're wrong on the last your first three reasons evaporate I take it. Your Honor that's correct. As far as this court goes that is absolutely correct. First of all geography. The government would have you focus on the fact that Long Island is an island. It's surrounded by water. That's reality. The states have never disputed that. But the reality is that that island forms a bay. It forms a very large bay. It encloses those waters. It is a unique island. It is a unique bay. The government referred to the charts in the back of their brief. You will notice that those charts only show you the Black Island Sound area. I submit that from their point of view that is what they would like to have you see. from our point of view and from reality we would like you first of all geographically to look at Long Island in total and Long Island Sound. In the back of the Masters report as Appendix B there is a chart which shows you that area. I suggest it is difficult to follow so we have provided you with an additional map a satellite map which you have before you and that map should you care to pursue it at some point will give you a better idea because of the contrast and the color of what that's correct Justice Springer. And what I would suggest that the first thing that you see is geographically that Long Island fits into the mainland and in fact geographically is closer to the mainland than the government would suggest. It is separated from the mainland by a body of water referred to as the East River and because it is separated by that body of water the government says it may not be considered as closely related to the mainland. Now this court in the Louisiana case suggested factors which should be considered in determining whether an island is realistically part of the mainland. The first of these factors is size. Long Island is a very large island. It is over 100 miles long. It has 450 miles of shoreline. It contains four counties of the state of New York. It contains two boroughs of the state of New York. Over half the city population is on that island. When you say four counties are you including among those the two boroughs? So it's two boroughs in Nassau and Suffolk counties. Yes, that is correct. Now the only I think the relevant thing about size is in relationship to the water that's enclosed. It's in relationship to the projection from the mainland. And I might also say that size is another consideration when the government talks about islands and mud lumps in the Mississippi, in the Delta area and in the Gulf. I would say to you that in my opinion, there is absolutely no comparison. The master looked at charts of that area. He looked at charts of islands in Alaska and there were no comparison. The next factor which this court said should be considered is distance from the mainland. Now the East River separates Long Island from the mainland. What are you talking about when you refer to the mainland? Manhattan? I'm talking about Manhattan and I'm also talking about the Bronx. The Bronx, I don't think there would be any dispute about that being the mainland. When the government says that the East River is seven-tenths of a mile wide, where is it measuring the East River? That, your honor, is measured from Throgsneck to Willits Point and that is not the narrowest point. If you went straight across from... That is Throgsneck to... That's just up to north end of Flushing. That's correct. Your Honor... I got it. That's the two-thirds of a mile. Yes, Justice Boyle. And how wide is it down at Manhattan? Well, it gets down to about three-tenths of a mile. On either side of... What's the island there? That would be... It slips my... On your map, the very narrowest point is the water on either side of an island. That... Well, it gets... I think that's referred to as Roosevelt Island. And how wide is the water passage there? Well, it would be less than three-tenths of a mile, Your Honor. But I think it gets narrower, even narrower farther than... Under the Convention, do you have to treat islands like that as water, however? Your Honor... I mean, you're not just... Isn't that what the Convention instructs us to do? Just so, Conor, it says to treat islands as water in terms of the measurement of water area for complying with the semicircle test. Mr. Claiborne suggested that the geographer of the United States Dr. Hodson had treated that as water. In fact, Exhibit 78, the deposition... I'm sorry, it's Exhibit 73, U.S. 73, is the deposition of Dr. Hodson. On page 78, he says that Manhattan would be considered a part of the mainland. And obviously you can see the connection there, the river between the two. But not Roosevelt Island. Not Roosevelt Island. No, Your Honor. Now, the... If Manhattan, if Long Island is a part of the mainland, is Roosevelt Island? Your Honor, Roosevelt Island is an island. We don't consider that part of the mainland. There's not a bridge running over there. It doesn't make any difference. It doesn't make any difference at all. The next factor is the depth and utility of the intervening waters. Your Honor, you've caught me out. The Queensborough Bridge goes across Roosevelt Island. You are exactly right. I was just getting ready to blow my brains out. You're exactly right. In fact, there's a tram car that runs from Manhattan, but you're exactly right. I didn't think of that, but you're exactly right. The depth and utility of the intervening waters. The waters of the East River are internal waters. Now, basically, the East River is a strait running between two bays. It runs between New York Harbor, and it runs between the waters of Long Island Sand. That opening into the East River at the end of Long Island Sand is dwarfed by the size of the water body. It's dwarfed by the size of the island. The depth, Mr. Claiborne suggests to you, is 34 feet, and that depth has been increased by a major project of the Corps of Engineers back in the 1980s. The shape is another factor. It's a long projection from the mainland enclosing a large body of water. Is that East River body of water substantially greater than that of other channels which this Court has previously ignored for purposes of determining a headland? Your Honor, I think it probably is. It certainly deeper, but I would suggest to your honor that that is greater navigability and deeper than any that we have previously ignored. That is correct, your honor, but I would suggest that that is relative here to the size of the island and to the size of the water bodies. There are also here, of course, physical connections to the mainland. You really think that we should follow a principle that says because you build a bridge you ought to be able to annex an island? Doesn't that have international ramifications that we might not like as a nation? Your honor, I... Under, in interpreting the Geneva Convention. I guess, O'Connor, I would suggest that that is one factor that this court considered. These are major physical connections. Well, isn't that kind of a risky factor on which to determine this question? Your honor, that is one additional factor that I would suggest, and I certainly wouldn't hinge the relationship on that as the only factor. Well, you think you can win even without that factor? That's correct, your honor. I say that we can win because of the close relationship between Long Island and the mainland that's geographically there, that is there by common sense, and is there because of the other factors which this court, which I have enumerated, and because the East River, in separating Long Island from the mainland, is, according to the government, the only reason that Long Island Sound can't be a bay is because that is not a river. None of those factors would change if, in fact, that was a river. So that is their distinction. And what I say is it's not a river, but it's also, it is an estuary. It's a very complex estuary, which their own witness, Dr. Swanson, testified to. And the Hudson River is an estuary. The convention would consider, obviously, estuaries in terms of bays, because we're talking about areas that are on the ocean. But let me just... Don't you think the fact that the government agrees, the Special Master found the government agrees that this is a historic bay, doesn't that support your argument that Manhattan or that Long Island is part of the mainland? Yeah, Your Honor, if you consider those are internal waters, this is why I would say they have, on occasion people have said that they recognize it as a historic bay, they only recognize it as historic waters. If, in fact, they recognize it as a historic bay, then they would have to go the other mile and say it was a juridical bay. But I think this court has said the best and most workable definition of a bay is the convention, and the convention, all the requirements of the convention were found by the master to apply to this area. Also, the whole concept in international law which permits a bay to be closed is the fact that it's an area that is surrounded by land, it is closely related to that land, and the reason it can be closed off is because by closing it off, you're not interfering with through international traffic going between two foreign states. And the master found that that was the situation here, that there was no through foreign commerce passing through this area. For all the reasons I have suggested, plus common sense, Long Island forms a bay. The master said if there is ever a situation where a large island will be considered a part of the mainland, so the waters enclosed between the island and the coast can be a juridical bay, this is it. Mr. Chief Justice, I may. Mr. Georgie. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. This is not a case of Rhode Island imperialism. We're certainly happy to be the smallest state, and we're happy to remain as such. However, we do not wish to have an Argo merchant accident on our shores, and because the Congress at the very beginning of this republic, in a law now codified as 46 U.S. Code, Section 211, saw fit to delegate to the various states the responsibility or the obligation, if they so chose, to regulate pilotage in their waters, in the bays, inlets, and harbors of the United States, then they could so do. And Rhode Island has chosen to do that, and that is the genesis of this litigation we have here today. A question earlier from the bench is certainly made reference to Ball v. Dunlap, which is pending on certiorari before this court in docket number 75-6990. And should we lose this case, should Block Island Sound and Long Island Sound not be found by this court to be a juridical bay. Rhode Island would no longer be able to regulate pilotage of foreign flag vessels and American vessels under foreign registry in Block Island Sound. This is not a small item. Super tankers navigate through Block Island Sound and into Long Island Sound, passing between the Rhode Island coast and Block Island. Then they go to Port Jefferson, where there's a major offload facility. Other smaller tankers, because of the draft in the East River, go down and dock and unload in the East River in the vicinity of LaGuardia Airport and those facilities there. So we're talking about a very serious issue to Rhode Island. Further, you say they go through Block Island Sound. That's correct. And then go down and come up through the narrows? No, they go through Block Island Sound, Justice Rehnquist. They then go through the race, which is between Fisher's Island and the number of small islands, Little Gull Island and Great Gull Island, and then they go down into Port Jefferson, which is on Long Island, which is on the north coast of Long Island, about midway down. And that's their point of destination? That's their point of destination. They also go to New Haven Harbor, where there are also major oil facilities there. Smaller tankers go to Shelter Harbor. They go through London. They go through smaller facilities in London, not as large as in New Haven, Justice White. This is traffic from foreign traffic headed for ports on the Sound than goes through Block Island Sound. Captain Neary was a Rhode Island witness, and there was testimony also from the United States, Dr. Swanson, I believe, which spoke of vessel movements. The predominant of vessels that enter Block Island Sound, they go to ports on Long Island Sound, and they go only as far as the East River. They don't navigate through the East River and then go up the Hudson to dock and unload there or go to New Jersey ports, ports, Bayonne and the like. Those vessels come in through lower New York Bay. So you're not talking about through traffic that's going up the Hudson River. They go outside. So that the international usage of this water is just not there. It's not there in the record, and I don't think the international implications, which you refer to, Justice Powell, are there in the record. They are this scepter that is raised in this sort of litigation. The impact of fisheries, the impact of coastal zone management is just not there in this case.
